Statistical significance was determined by Brown–Forsythe and Welch ANOVA with two-sided Dunnett’s T3 multiple comparisons test (d,f) and one-way ANOVA followed by a two-sided Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test (g,h). *P < 0.05 and **P < 0.01 indicate statistically significant differences. Gel source data are shown in Supplementary Fig. 25.

Recent findings suggest that performance of EpTFIIAγ rice and maize lines was tested in the field over multiple seasons. Two-year evaluation (2023 and 2024) of rice in Hanzhong (Shaanxi Province) found that plant height, grain yield per plant, grain size (ratio of grain length to width) and 1,000-grain weight were all increased in the transgenic lines compared with wild-type controls under full-irrigation conditions, and this difference was more pronounced under water deficit (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12c,e). EpTFIIAγ rice had 10.2–11.9% increases in grain yield per plant under full irrigation and 19.7–24.1% increases under water-deficit conditions relative to wild-type Nipponbare. EpTFIIAγ maize was examined over 3-year (2023–2025) field trials in Zhangye (Gansu Province), Changji and Aksu (Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region), which are arid regions and vital maize production areas (Supplementary Fig. 5). All EpTFIIAγ maize lines were taller than wild-type B73 under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions, although grain number per ear, yield per plant and 100-grain weight were only increased under water-limited conditions (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 12d,f,g). Grain yield per plant increased by a striking 27.9–37.2% in Zhangye (Extended Data Fig. 12f), 31.9–42.4% in Changji (Fig. 5h) and 31.1–35.4% in Aksu (Extended Data Fig. 12g) under water-limited conditions. Although growth duration of EpTFIIAγ plants remained comparable with that of wild-type controls under full irrigation, drought stress was accompanied by a 3–5-day delay in rice maturation and 2–4-day longer time to maturity in maize (Extended Data Fig. 12h,i). These cumulative results indicated that transgenic expression of EpTFIIAγ consistently and substantially improved drought resistance and yield of major cereal crops.

Using multifunctional, pleiotropic genes to simultaneously modulate multiple pathways could potentially streamline genetic improvement efforts aimed at enhancing crop stress resistance and yield16,46. Here we demonstrate that transgenic expression of EpTFIIAγ synergistically enhances both drought resistance and yield in cereal crops. In field trials, transgenic wheat and rice expressing EpTFIIAγ had greater yield and biomass production than respective wild-type controls across full water availability and water-deficit conditions (Fig. 5g, Extended Data Fig. 12e and Supplementary Fig. 7). In maize, these benefits were exclusively observed under water-deficit conditions (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 12f,g), whereas the lack of a yield response under well-watered conditions could potentially reflect functional redundancy in regulating grain production in C4 species with high metabolic efficiency and strict constraints on reproductive synchrony47,48. Plants expressing EpTFIIAγ consistently demonstrated higher drought resistance and grain yield than wild-type counterparts across different genetic backgrounds and cultivars (Fig. 1, Supplementary Tables 1–6 and Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7). Moreover, EpTFIIAγ expression also confers resistance to other major stressors, including excessive heat, lodging and stripe rust (Extended Data Fig. 2), indicating that the inverse relationship between stress resistance and yield can be decoupled or even reversed.

Recent findings suggest that although used as a transgene expressed in cereal crops, EpTFIIAγ was isolated from E. pusillum, an extremophile fungus adapted to drought-prone conditions24. The N-terminal IDR of EpTFIIAγ endows it with unique functions in plants, enabling binding to TATA-box-containing motifs and physical interactions with endogenous transcriptional activators (Figs. 3a,b and 4a–e and Supplementary Fig. 22). By contrast, plant TFIIAγ homologues are restricted to basal transcriptional initiation and do not appear to mediate drought responses (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 6). IDRs are known to mediate LLPS49, yet EpTFIIAγ did not detectably undergo LLPS (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 19). Instead, its IDR is thought to undergo transient, weak DNA interactions that emerge as precise localization patterns on chromatin50,51. This mechanism allows EpTFIIAγ to integrate into the plant regulatory network for coordinately targeting pathways involved in transcriptional regulation, stress and hormone responses, transpiration, photosynthesis, chlorophyll biosynthesis, sugar transport and grain filling, ultimately enhancing drought resistance and grain yield under greenhouse and field conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Fig. 24).

According to recent reports, crucially, enhanced photosynthesis in flag leaves and grain starch accumulation under well-watered conditions, together with a slightly longer growth cycle under drought, suggest that EpTFIIAγ improves yield by increasing source-to-sink transport of photoassimilates, thereby promoting starch biosynthesis during the 5–15-day period after pollination (Fig. 2, Extended Data Figs. 3–5 and Supplementary Figs. 7f,l and 12–17). Improved carbon assimilation in EpTFIIAγ plants did not promote root development under well-watered conditions, but did lead to enhanced root growth under drought stress (Fig. 2h–j). In this context, we propose that excess photoassimilates are preferentially allocated to aboveground biomass under non-limiting water conditions, whereas drought stress triggers ABA signalling to redirect carbon flux towards the roots to enhance water absorption and retention37. Several lines of evidence support the hypothesis that EpTFIIAγ confers drought resistance and yield enhancement in wheat through the following pathways: (1) ameliorating drought resistance and WUE through TaDREB1C; (2) boosting photosynthesis, biomass and grain yield through TaCOG1 and TaCol-B5; (3) enhancing photosynthetic assimilation and grain filling through TaCIN2; and (4) interacting with several transcriptional activators to enhance the expression of target genes (Fig. 4, Extended Data Figs. 9–11 and Supplementary Fig. 23). These synergistic effects reproducibly conferred enhanced plant fitness and yield for all three cereal crops. Next steps include introducing EpTFIIAγ into contemporary, farmer-preferred rice cultivars and elite maize hybrid backgrounds, as well as exploring functionality in other staple crops not adapted to drought.

Recent findings suggest that heterologous expression of other extremophile transgenes can also improve resistance to abiotic stressors in Arabidopsis or tobacco, such as EpANN from E. pusillum52, versatile peroxidase from Bjerkandera adusta53 and hsp70/Thkel1 from Trichoderma harzianum54. However, whether these genes can improve stress resistance in cereals has not been reported, and mechanisms for regulating resistance remain poorly understood. Given the restrictions on transgenic plants in some growing regions, it may be possible to enhance crop drought resilience without genetic modification by targeting pathways controlled by EpTFIIAγ through chemical or biological strategies. For example, certain ABA receptor agonists can mimic ABA signalling to trigger stomatal closure and stress responses55,56,57. A photoactivatable T6P precursor overcomes source and sink limitations under diverse conditions, boosting wheat yields by 5–17%8. Certain symbiotic fungi (for example, Trichoderma) secrete metabolites that can induce systemic drought resistance58,59,60. Although these strategies circumvent certain biosafety concerns associated with transgenics, their transient and environment-dependent efficacy potentially increases long-term costs. Transgenic approaches provide durable and heritable resistance, thereby lowering costs. In agricultural practice, combining genetic engineering with certain chemical and/or biological treatments may lead to synergistic improvements in yield and stress mitigation.

Recent findings suggest that despite these advances, solutions remain urgently needed to overcome obstacles of diminishing arable land and intensifying climate change while doubling global food production by 2050. This study demonstrates the potential to substantially improve yields among the major staple crops, despite centuries of previous breeding efforts, at least in countries where genetically modified plants can be grown. Beyond demonstrating that EpTFIIAγ can dramatically boost productivity by enhancing drought resistance and grain yield, our study unveils a conserved mechanism for orchestrating stress responses, development, photosynthesis and yield to ultimately decouple antagonistic regulatory pathways. These findings open new avenues for engineering plant growth and stress resilience by key factors such as EpTFIIAγ.

Industry observers note that wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) plants were grown under both controlled environments or field conditions. For controlled environments, wheat seeds were immersed in a 70% (v/v) ethanol for 2 min. Afterwards, the seeds were rinsed three times with sterile distilled water to remove any residual ethanol. The surface-sterilized seeds were then stratified at 4 °C in darkness for 3 days, followed by germination under white light (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance) at room temperature. Germinated seedlings were planted in a mixture of nutrient soil and vermiculite (3:1) and maintained in a controlled growth chamber (LRX-2000D-LED, Ningbo Prandt Instrument) under 200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 14 °C and 12 °C day and night temperature cycle with 60% humidity. Field trials were conducted in China with uniform wheat seeds sown at a daily average temperature of 15–20 °C (usually in October). Detailed information for each experimental site is provided in Supplementary Fig. 5. Specifically, EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat and wild-type controls were planted in Yangling (Shaanxi Province, 34° 16′ N, 108° 04′ E) during 2023–2025, and three other arid regions with an annual rainfall of 120–250 mm in 2025, including Heyang (Shaanxi Province, 35° 43′ N, 110° 02′ E), Cangzhou (Hebei Province, 38° 33′ N, 116° 38′ E) and Linfen (Shanxi Province, 36° 56′ N, 112° 34′ E). In each experimental field, basal fertilizers were applied at a rate of 37,500–45,000 kg ha–1 decomposed organic fertilizer, 600–750 kg ha–1 compound fertilizer with 1:1:1 of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), 22.5 kg ha–1 zinc sulfate and 7.5 kg ha–1 borax. All fertilizers were thoroughly mixed and incorporated into the soil during plowing to ensure uniform distribution in the plow layer. At the Yangling site, full-irrigation and water-limited growth conditions were established, with the water-limited condition implemented using a rain-out shelter and controlled irrigation. After initial irrigation at sowing by a drip irrigation system, water-limited plots received approximately 30% of the water volume supplied to full-irrigation plots for the rest of the growing season. At the other sites, local wheat production management was applied after an initial thorough watering at sowing.

In a recent development, phenotypic characterization of rice (O. sativa) was conducted at the seedling stage under controlled conditions and at the mature stage under field conditions. For seedling-stage assessment, seeds were surface sterilized using a 10% (v/v) sodium hypochlorite solution and incubated in darkness at 37 °C for 3 days, followed by germination under white light (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance). Germinated seeds were transplanted into a mixture of Pindstrup turf and vermiculite (1:1) and cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance, 14-h light and 10-h dark photoperiod, 28 °C and 26 °C day and night temperature cycle and 60% humidity. For scoring at the maturity stage under field conditions, seedlings with healthy and uniform appearance were transplanted into paddy fields in Hanzhong (Shaanxi Province, 33.04° N, 107.01° E) in early June. Basal fertilizer was applied at 30,000 kg ha–1 decomposed farmyard manure, 450 kg ha–1 ammonium bicarbonate, 225 kg ha–1 potassium chloride and 375 kg ha–1 superphosphate. The field was rotavated to mix the fertilizer evenly with the soil, then flooded to maintain a 3–5-cm water layer. Transplanting followed a spacing regime of 30 cm between rows; each transgenic line and control were planted in five rows with ten plants per row and 20 cm between individual seedlings. Within 7 days post-transplanting, a 3–5-cm shallow water layer was maintained to promote seedling recovery. From the end of seedling recovery to the tillering stage, the water layer was adjusted to 2–3 cm. From the booting stage to ripening, a 3–4-cm shallow water layer was retained until rice maturity. Drought-stress treatment was applied by halting irrigation and draining standing water at the booting stage (panicle elongation). Irrigation was resumed to allow recovery after irreversible leaf-rolling symptoms were observed for 5 consecutive days in the experimental group. For each genotype, at least three biological replicates were grown under each treatment condition.

Cultivation and propagation of maize (Z. mays) were carried out in field plots at Northwest A&F University (Yangling, 34° 16′ N, 108° 04′ E) during 2021–2022, and self-pollination was performed to obtain homozygous lines. For seedling-stage experiments under controlled conditions, seeds were sown in nursery pots filled with a 3:1 mixture of nutrient soil and vermiculite, and cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 25 °C and 23 °C day and night temperature cycle and 60% relative humidity. For phenotyping at the maturity stage under field conditions, plants were in experimental fields in Zhangye (Gansu Province, 38.56° N, 100.26° E) from May–September in 2023, Changji (Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, 43.06° N, 86.18° E) from May–September in 2024 and Aksu (Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, 41.71° N, 80.81° E) from May–September in 2025. Maize lines were sown in accordance with the local cropping season, maintaining uniformity in planting density, irrigation, fertilizer application and pest control treatments. Each genotype had four replicate plots (4 rows × 13 seeds) under full-irrigation and drought treatments, respectively. To mitigate border effects, each plot was surrounded by dedicated buffer rows, thereby ensuring uniform conditions among plants used for data collection. Drought treatment was imposed from the V5 stage (fifth leaf with visible ligule) until completion of silking, during which the soil water potential gradually decreased from −20 to −220 kPa. Watering was typically applied using a drip irrigation system at approximately 10-day intervals, with drought-treated plots receiving approximately 40% of the water volume supplied to well-watered controls. Buried Watermark 200SS sensors were used to monitor and maintain soil water potential (0 to −20 kPa) in plots treated with full irrigation. Following harvest, dried ears were assessed for yield per plant and kernels per ear.

Recent findings suggest that to generate transgenic lines either heterologously expressing EpTFIIAγ or overexpressing TaTFIIAγ, TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaWRKY46, TaVOZ1, TaDREB1C, TaCOG1 and TaCIN2 in wheat, respective coding sequences were cloned into the pCAMBIA3301 vector under the control of the Ubiquitin promoter and NOS terminator. For CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing of TaARF6 and TaWRKY46, single guide RNAs targeting exons were designed using E-CRISP (http://www.e-crisp.org/), cloned into the pBUE411 vector via BsaI restriction sites, and verified by Sanger sequencing25. Constructs were then introduced into Agrobacterium tumefaciens EHA105 and transformed into immature embryos of wheat cvs. Fielder, XN979, XN511, JM22 and XZ9104 following established protocols61. Transgenic T0 plants were identified by PCR and transgene expression was confirmed either by RT–qPCR or by western blotting. Positive T0 plants were propagated to the T2 or T3 generation in a greenhouse for subsequent phenotyping and trait scoring. Primers used are provided in the Supplementary Table 15 and antibodies are described below.

For O. sativa cv. Nipponbare transformation, the EpTFIIAγ coding region was cloned into the pBWA(V)HS vector under the control of the Cauliflower Mosaic Virus 35S (CaMV 35S) promoter and CaMV 35S-polyA terminator. The construct was introduced into A. tumefaciens EHA105, and transformation into immature embryos of Nipponbare. Transgenic T0 plants were identified by PCR, and transgene expression was confirmed by either RT–qPCR or western blotting. Positive T0 plants were propagated to the T3 generation in a greenhouse for subsequent phenotyping and trait scoring.

According to recent reports, for Z. mays inbred line B73 transformation, the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pBCXUN vector48 under the control of the maize Ubiquitin promoter and NOS terminator. The construct was introduced into A. tumefaciens EHA105 and subsequently delivered into immature embryos following established protocols48. T1 seeds were screened by PCR, and homozygous T3 lines were used for phenotypic analysis.

Recent findings suggest that for generation of transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana in the Col-0 background, the full-length coding regions of EpTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were cloned into the pGreen-0029 vector62 under the CaMV 35S promoter and NOS terminator, introduced into A. tumefaciens GV3101, and transformed using the floral-dip method63. T1 seeds were screened on half-strength Murashige and Skoog (1/2 MS) medium with 50 mg l−1 kanamycin, and homozygous T3 lines were used for phenotypic analysis.

Recent findings suggest that for wheat, seeds from wild-type and three T3 transgenic lines were sown side by side in nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture in plastic boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height), and cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity for approximately 30 days. Drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days until the soil volumetric water content reached approximately 3% and was maintained at this level for an additional 5 days. Survival rates were assessed 3 days after rewatering by scoring all plants with green and viable leaves. At least 16 plants per genotype were analysed across three or four biological replicates.

Recent findings suggest that for rice, Nipponbare controls and T3 transgenic seeds were germinated in darkness at 37 °C for 3 days, and subsequently transferred to white light. Germinated seeds were then planted side by side in a mixture of Pindstrup turf and vermiculite (1:1, w/w) in plastic boxes (35 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm, length × width × height), and cultivated in a growth chamber under the same growth conditions as wheat, but with a 28 °C and 26 °C day and night temperature cycle. After approximately 30 days of growth, drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 21 days until the soil volumetric water content reached approximately 3%, then maintaining this level for an additional 5 days. To assess stress resistance, survival rates were recorded 3 days after rewatering by scoring all plants with green, viable leaves. At least 16 plants per line were analysed across three biological replicates.

For maize, wild-type B73 and three independent T3 transgenic lines were grown side by side in boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height) filled with a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture. After germination, seedlings were cultivated under the same environmental conditions as wheat, except using a 25 °C and 23 °C day and night temperature regime. At the three-leaf stage, drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days, followed by rewatering. Survival rates were assessed 7 days later by scoring all plants with green and viable leaves. At least 16 plants per line were analysed across three biological replicates.

Industry observers note that for Arabidopsis, surface-sterilized seeds were sown on half-strength MS medium, stratified in the dark at 4 °C for 3 days, and then transferred to a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 22 °C and 20 °C day and night temperature cycle, 60% humidity and a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod. After 7 days, seedlings were transferred to pots containing a 2:1 Jiffy mix:vermiculite soil mixture. After approximately 21 days of growth, drought stress was applied by withholding water for 14 days. Survival rates were assessed 3 days after rewatering by scoring all plants with green and viable leaves. At least 16 plants per line were analysed across three biological replicates.

Seeds of EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants and wild-type controls were sown in 7 cm × 10 cm pots containing a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture and grown in a growth chamber. At the three-leaf stage, seedlings were exposed to 42 °C for 36 h and allowed to recover at 23 °C for 4 days. Seedling survival rates were calculated based on the number of individual plants with green, viable shoots. At least nine seedlings per genotype were analysed per assay, with three independent experiments. Maximum photochemical efficiency of photosystem II (Fv/Fm) was measured using a FluorPen FP110 fluorometer (PSI). Electrolyte leakage was determined using a conductivity meter (DDSJ-307F, Shanghai INESA Scientific Instruments). Relative electrolyte conductivity (%) was calculated as (C1 – C0)/(C2 – C0) × 100%, where C1 represents initial conductivity before boiling, C2 is the final conductivity after boiling and C0 is the conductivity of deionized water.

Wild-type Fielder and EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants were cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Three-week-old seedlings were inoculated with Pst urediniospores and maintained in darkness at 12 °C and 100% relative humidity for 24 h, after which plants were returned to standard growth conditions. Disease phenotypes were evaluated following the development of stripe rust symptoms. Relative fungal biomass was quantified by qPCR analysis of the ratio of Pst-specific PstEF transcripts relative to that of the wheat reference gene, TaEF64, in CTAB-extracted genomic DNA.

For histological analyses, reactive oxygen species accumulation was visualized by staining infected leaves with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (1 mg ml−1). Stained samples were examined using a BX-51 microscope (Olympus). Stomata associated with haustorial mother-cell formation were defined as successful infection sites, and the 3,3′-diaminobenzidine-stained area at each site was quantified using CellSens Entry software (Olympus). At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point. Fungal infection structures were visualized by WGA–Alexa Fluor 488 staining (20 μg ml−1; Amresco) following tissue clearing and alkali treatment. Samples were mounted in 50% glycerol and examined using an Olympus BX-53 fluorescence microscope equipped with a GFP filter set. Substomatal vesicles, infection hyphae and other fungal structures were observed, and hyphal length and fungal colonization area were quantified using CellSens Entry software. At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point.

In a recent development, wheat drought resistance at the maturity stage was evaluated under full-irrigation (that is, control) and water-limited conditions in the field. Each plot measured 5 m × 2 m and consisted of 25 rows, with 20-cm spacing between rows and 10 cm between plants. Control plots were irrigated regularly throughout the entire growing season, and water-limited plots were isolated using a 1.5-m-deep underground waterproof barrier and covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation. After the initial irrigation at sowing, water-limited plots received approximately 30% of the water volume applied to the well-watered plots for the remainder of the season.

According to recent reports, photosynthetic parameters of wheat were recorded with a LI-6400XT portable photosynthesis system (LI-COR) at four Zadoks growth stages from tillering (Z25) to milk development (Z75). Net photosynthesis rate (Pn), transpiration rate (Tr), stomatal conductance (Gs) and instantaneous water use efficiency (calculated as Pn/Tr) were measured from at least 15 plants per line. Light-response and CO2-response curves were fitted using the Farquhar–von Caemmerer–Berry model to estimate maximum carboxylation rate (Vcmax) and maximum electron transport rate (Jmax). Chlorophyll fluorescence (Fv/Fm) and SPAD values were measured using a hand-held chlorophyll-fluorescence measurement instrument (FluorPen FP 110, FluorCam) and chlorophyll meter (SPAD-502, Konica Minolta), respectively. Leaf area of the main tiller was measured using a leaf-area meter (Yaxin-1242, Dianjiang Technology). Agronomic traits, including plant height, spike number, spike length, spikelet number, grain number per spike, grain length, grain width, 1,000-grain weight, yield per plant, biomass and harvest index were measured from 50–100 plants per line. Grains were oven-dried at 37 °C before yield quantification.

Rice agronomic traits were evaluated in the field at maturity. Seeds were sown in a seedling nursery and transplanted into the field at 25 days after sowing. A wide–narrow row-planting pattern was adopted in the field, with 5 rows × 10 plants per plot. Each line was randomly assigned to three plots (that is, three biological replicates). Water-limited plots were covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation, and drought stress was initiated at booting stage by withholding irrigation and opening drainage valves to remove standing water. Drought treatment was terminated and followed by a rewatering recovery phase once either the experimental or control plants revealed irreversible leaf-rolling symptoms that persisted for 5 consecutive days. At maturity, each plant was harvested individually. Traits assessed included plant height, grain size, 1,000-grain weight and grain yield per plant.

In a recent development, maize field trials were conducted at the three abovementioned locations under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions. Drought treatment was applied through artificial irrigation control using a drip irrigation system equipped with underground Watermark 200SS sensors to monitor and maintain soil water potential. Each treatment included four replicate plots (2.6 m wide; 0.4 m row spacing), with four rows per line. Agronomic traits, including plant height, grain number per ear, yield per plant and 100-grain weight, were measured following open pollination.

Wheat lodging resistance was evaluated using the second basal internode of the main tiller. Stem breaking strength was measured at 10 days after anthesis using a plant stem strength tester (IN-JG2, Shandong Holder Electronic Technology). Stem diameter was measured on the same internode using a digital caliper. Each stem was measured three times, and 20 biological replicates were analysed for each genotype.

Sources indicate that for stem histology, the middle region of the peduncle internode was collected at 15 days post-anthesis and fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and clearing in xylene, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections (6–8 μm) were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems) and subjected to safranin–fast green double staining. In brief, sections were stained with safranin, differentiated in 90% ethanol, counterstained with fast green, cleared in a 1:1 (v/v) xylene–ethanol mixture and mounted. Panoramic images were acquired using SlideViewer software (v2.9.0), and stem diameter, vascular bundle number and mechanical tissue thickness were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

According to recent reports, for seedling-stage stress experiments, germinated wheat seedlings were grown in 7 cm × 7 cm × 10 cm pots with Hoagland’s modified nutrient solution for 3 days under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Subsequently, the control group was continuously cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution, whereas the drought-stress group was cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution containing 20% (w/v) PEG6000. Seedlings in both groups were grown for 3–4 weeks, with the culture solution replaced every 3 days, after which root parameters were scored. The root system of each seedling was excised, lateral roots were separated from nodes, evenly spread in a transparent plastic tray with 0.5 cm of deionized water, and intertwined fine lateral branches were gently separated with forceps to avoid overlap. Primary root length, root fresh weight and root dry weight were measured manually.

Recent findings suggest that wheat plants were grown in PVC columns (150 cm × 15 cm) filled with soil under well-watered and water-limited (water supply terminated at the jointing stage) conditions, with one plant per column. When wheat reached the grain-filling stage, the soil and root system were carefully removed from the columns. Roots were rinsed with running water to remove adhering soil and impurities, then excised from shoots. Root length was measured immediately after cleaning. Subsequently, roots were placed in paper envelopes and dried in a forced-air drying oven at 65 °C for 7 days, after which root dry weight was determined.

Recent findings suggest that water loss assays were performed on 4-week-old wheat seedlings as previously described25. Fully expanded third leaves were excised and immediately weighed to record their initial fresh weight (FW0). Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper under ambient room conditions (22–25 °C, 40–60% relative humidity, with light exposure) without covering. Fresh weight (FWt) was recorded at regular intervals. Water loss was expressed as a percentage of the initial fresh weight using the formula: Water loss rate (%) = [(FW0 − FWt)/FW0] × 100. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Industry observers note that water loss assays on Arabidopsis were carried out as previously described65. In brief, fully expanded rosette leaves from 3-week-old plants were detached at the same time of day to minimize circadian effects. The initial fresh weight (FW0) was recorded immediately using a precision analytical balance. Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper in a controlled environment (22 °C, 50–60% relative humidity, no direct airflow). Fresh weights (FWt) were measured at specified time intervals, typically every 30 or 60 min for 6 h. Water loss rate was calculated using the same formula as for wheat. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Infrared thermography was performed on 4-week-old greenhouse-grown seedlings that were subjected to 15 days of water withholding, during which soil water content was maintained at approximately 50% of well-watered capacity. Leaf surface temperatures under different treatments were recorded using a FLIR A655sc infrared camera (Teledyne FLIR). Thermal images were analysed using FLIR ResearchIR Max (v4.40) to quantify temperature differences and assess drought-induced physiological responses.

According to recent reports, to evaluate photosynthesis-related changes, multispectral imaging was conducted using the PhenoBox live-plant multispectral imaging analysis system (LemnaTec GmbH). Five-leaf-stage wheat seedlings were individually cultivated in plots filled with nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture under controlled growth-chamber conditions. Imaging was performed under three distinct soil-moisture regimes, including well watered (soil water content maintained at approximately 90%), mild drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 50%) and severe drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 30%). Four surface multispectral images were captured for each plant. Standardized imaging protocols were applied to ensure consistent lighting and sensor calibration. Two spectral values, normalized water index and normalized difference vegetation index, were used to assess plant water status and physiological responses under drought stress: normalized water index = (R970 – R850)/(R970 + R850) and normalized difference vegetation index = (R800 – R670)/(R800 + R670), with R representing reflectance and numbers referring to wavelength (nm).

For chlorophyll fluorescence measurements, imaging was performed using the live-plant imaging system CV-200 produced by Beijing Feizhi Technology and controlled by CropVision_Controller_v2 software. Fluorescence images were captured under stable-lighting conditions at the same time points used for multispectral imaging. The effective ΦPSII was automatically extracted using the software and was used to evaluate photosynthetic performance and drought-stress responses in wheat seedlings across the different water treatments.

Industry observers note that stomatal density measurements were performed following a published protocol66. To determine stomatal density in wheat, the middle region of the abaxial surface of the fully expanded second leaf of seedlings was selected for analysis. The abaxial epidermis was carefully adhered to a piece of transparent adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll tissue were then gently scraped off using a razor blade. The tape carrying the intact abaxial epidermal cells was subsequently mounted on a standard microscope slide (75 mm × 25 mm) for microscopic observation. A minimum of ten slides were prepared for each wheat line. Stomata were observed and photographed using compound microscope (Olympus IX71) under a ×10 objective lens, and stomatal density was calculated as the number of stomata per unit area of the field of view.

For Arabidopsis, fully expanded and healthy functional leaves (typically the fifth or sixth true leaf) were selected. The abaxial surface of each leaf was gently pressed onto clear adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll were carefully removed using a razor blade, leaving the lower epidermis adhered to the tape. The tape carrying the epidermal imprint was then mounted smoothly onto a standard glass slide (75 mm × 25 mm), avoiding air bubbles. At least ten slides were prepared per line for analysis.

Stomatal aperture measurements in wheat and Arabidopsis were determined following established protocols65. For wheat, a fully expanded second leaf was excised and incubated in stomatal opening buffer containing 0.05 M KNO3, 10 mM MES and 50 μM CaCl2 (pH 6.15) under light conditions (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1, 25 °C) for 1.5 h or in darkness for 1 h. Leaves were then exposed to drought treatment under ambient air for 10 min, followed by incubation in continuous light, continuous dark or a light-to-dark transition for 30 min. The abaxial surface was carefully blot dried and adhered to transparent tape, and the adaxial epidermis and mesophyll cells were gently removed using a razor blade. The exposed abaxial epidermal layer on the tape was then mounted on a microscope slide for imaging. For Arabidopsis, the fifth or sixth rosette leaves were harvested and incubated in MES buffer (10 mM MES-KOH, pH 6.15, 10 mM KCl and 50 μM CaCl2) in a light incubator for 2.5 h to induce stomatal opening. The leaves were subsequently transferred to MES buffer containing 20% w/v PEG6000 and incubated for 2 h. Epidermal strips were prepared and imaged using a compound microscope (Olympus IX71). Stomatal aperture was defined as the width of the pore between the two guard cells, and the stomatal aperture ratio (width:length) was measured using ImageJ (v1.8.0). Data for each ecotype were collected from a minimum of 100 stomata.

Wheat seedlings were grown under controlled conditions until the three-leaf stage. Once soil moisture content declined below 30%, leaf samples were collected at designated intervals. Each genotype comprised three biological replicates, with each sample weighing no less than 1.5 g. Samples were placed in dry envelopes and dried in a constant-temperature forced-air oven at 60 °C until completely desiccated. The dried tissue was then ground into a fine powder for carbon isotope analysis using the stable-isotope ratio mass spectrometry method. Ground samples were treated with 4 mol dm−3 HCl for 24 h, then washed with deionized water until neutral, dried, ground and sieved through a 60-mesh screen. Approximately 0.4 mg of the solid sample was accurately weighed, placed into a tin cup and hermetically sealed, and placed in a 96-well plate. Isotopic measurements were conducted using a Flash 1112 Elemental Analyzer coupled to a Delta V Plus Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Finnigan). The carbon isotope ratio (δ13C) was calculated relative to the Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB) international standard using the formula: δ13C (‰) = [(Rsample/RVPDB) – 1] × 1,000, where R is the ratio of 13C to 12C. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Uniform wheat seeds were germinated at room temperature for 3 days and subsequently grown in half-strength Hoagland’s nutrient solution for 1 week. Seedlings were then subjected to either control conditions or drought stress induced by 15% (w/v) PEG6000. After 10 days of treatment, leaf and root tissues were harvested, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Three independent biological replicates were collected for each treatment. Hormone quantification was performed by Metware Biotechnology using an AB Sciex QTRAP 6500 LC–MS/MS system.

It has been revealed that wheat seeds were sown side by side in plastic boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height) filled with a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture. Seedlings were cultured under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 14 °C and 12 °C day and night temperature and 60% relative humidity for approximately 30 days (three-leaf stage). Drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days until leaf wilting was observed. Leaves were collected from at least three individual plants under well-watered and drought-stressed conditions. The activity of RuBisCO, along with the contents of chlorophyll, soluble sugars, sucrose, glucose and starch were measured using commercial assay kits all obtained from Solarbio: BC0445 for RuBisCO activity, BC0995 for chlorophyll, BC2460 for sucrose, BC0030 for soluble sugars, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch, all following the manufacturer’s instructions. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Industry observers note that to evaluate wheat grain development and filling dynamics, main tiller spikes were tagged before anthesis. Under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions, grains from the six central spikelets of each tagged spike were sampled at 5-day intervals from anthesis to physiological maturity, with a minimum of nine spikes collected per genotype per time point. Grain length, width and thickness were measured in 60–100 grains with a digital caliper (0.01-mm resolution); fresh weight was determined for 100-grain samples. Dry weight was obtained by drying samples at 80 °C to a constant weight following a 30-min pre-treatment at 105 °C. The mean grain-filling rate was calculated as the final grain dry weight divided by the grain-filling duration, expressed as mg per grain per day.

Flag leaf sheaths and developing grains were harvested at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 days after flowering. Soluble sugars (sucrose, fructose and glucose) and starch contents were quantified using commercial assay kits from Solarbio (BC2460 for sucrose, BC6360 for fructose, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch). Enzymatic activity assays were conducted using kits for sucrose synthase (SUS; BC0585), cell-wall invertase (CWI; BC4325) and ADP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (AGPase; BC0435) following the manufacturer’s protocols. All assays were performed with at least three independent biological replicates.

For grain histology, developing grains were collected from central spikelets at 15 days after flowering, then fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution (G2355, Solarbio) at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and xylene clearing, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections of 6–8 μm thickness were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems). For histological analysis, sections were stained with toluidine blue, whereas starch granules were visualized using periodic acid–Schiff reagent. Images were acquired using SlideViewer panoramic scanning software (v2.9.0). Grain cell size, cell number and starch granule number were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. First-strand complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from 1 μg of DNase-treated RNA using the HiScript reverse transcription kit (R223-01, Vazyme). RT–qPCR was performed in a 20-μl reaction volume containing 1.4 μl cDNA (pre-diluted to a concentration of 200 ng μl−1), 0.4 μM primers and 10 μl of SYBR Green Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme), using a CFX96 real-time PCR system (Bio-Rad). Gene-expression levels were calculated using the \({2}^{-\Delta \Delta {{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{T}}}}\) method67 with TaActin1 (TraesCS1B01G283900) serving as the reference gene for normalization. Primer sequences used for RT–qPCR are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

Recent findings suggest that the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Δhog1 mutant, which is sensitive to osmotic stress and lacks a functional copy of a gene encoding a high osmolarity glycerol 1 protein kinase (HOG1)68, was used to assess the drought-resistance function of TFIIAγ proteins. Coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were amplified via PCR using primers with flanking attB sites. These fragments were first cloned into the pDONR221 entry vector (Invitrogen) via BP recombination using the Gateway cloning system and subsequently transferred into the pGAD426 destination vector (Addgene) through an LR (attL and attR) recombination reaction. Recombinant plasmids were transformed into Δhog1 cells using the Frozen-EZ Yeast Transformation Kit (Zymo Research). Transformed strains were selected on synthetic dropout medium lacking uracil (SD−Ura). The pGAD426-GUS plasmid was used as a control.

For stress-tolerance assays, 10 μl of yeast culture (OD600 nm = 0.6) was spotted onto SD−Ura solid medium supplemented with 0.75 M sorbitol and incubated at 28 °C for 3 days. Growth in SD−Ura liquid medium containing 0.75 M sorbitol was monitored by measuring OD600 nm at 24-h intervals.

It has been revealed that the full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ (excluding translational stop codons) were cloned in-frame into the N-terminal region of the pJIT163-GFP expression vectors64, both driven by the CaMV 35S promoter. The resulting fusion constructs were introduced into wheat protoplasts (pJIT163-TFIIAγ-GFP). Transformed wheat protoplasts were incubated for 16 h to permit transient expression. GFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and an emission wavelength range of 500–530 nm. Nuclei were labelled with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), and fluorescence signal was verified to originate solely from intact fusion proteins via anti-GFP western blot.

Recent findings suggest that fluorescence imaging was conducted in wheat protoplasts and N. benthamiana epidermal cells transiently expressing EpTFIIAγ–GFP. To induce drought-stress-related or osmotic stress-related cellular responses, cells were treated with 10% (w/v) PEG8000, 1.5 M sorbitol, 50 μM ABA or 250 mM NaCl as indicated. Imaging was performed with an FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus). GFP fluorescence was excited at 488 nm and emission was captured at 491–535 nm. Image acquisition and processing were performed using FV31S-SW software.

According to recent reports, molecular dynamics of EpTFIIAγ–GFP condensates were characterized through FRAP assays. Selected condensates were photobleached using a 488-nm laser, and fluorescence recovery was monitored by timelapse imaging. Recovery curves were normalized to both pre-bleach intensity and the fluorescence of adjacent unbleached regions to correct for background photobleaching; data were analysed with FV31S-SW software. Molecular mobility of EpTFIIAγ and the IDR deletion variant was assessed by FCS analysis in wheat protoplasts. Autocorrelation curves were acquired from multiple cells and fitted to appropriate diffusion models using CorTector NanoX FCS software to obtain diffusion coefficients and molecular concentrations.

Sources indicate that to identify proteins that can potentially physically interact with EpTFIIAγ, a yeast two-hybrid screen was performed. The full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ was cloned into the pGBKT7 vector and served as the bait construct, fused to the binding domain of GAL4. The resulting pGBKT7-EpTFIIAγ plasmid was co-transformed with a pGADT7-based cDNA library (from wheat cv. Chinese Spring seedlings) into S. cerevisiae strain AH109 using the lithium acetate method, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Clontech). Positive clones were selected on selective dropout media, and candidate-interacting proteins were identified by PCR amplification and subsequent DNA sequencing.

To validate putative physical interactions between EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ with candidate partners, the coding sequences lacking translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were individually cloned into the pGADT7 vector to form prey constructs. The coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were used as bait in the pGBKT7 vector. Bait and prey constructs were co-transformed into S. cerevisiae AH109 using the lithium-acetate method. Protein–protein interactions were assessed by spotting serial tenfold dilutions of co-transformed yeast cultures onto SD/–Trp–Leu and SD/–Trp–Leu–His–Ade selective media.

To perform luciferase-complementation imaging assays, the coding sequences of TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaAKS1, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were cloned upstream of the nLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-nLUC vector, whereas EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were cloned downstream of the cLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-cLUC vector. These constructs were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and cultured overnight. The bacterial suspensions were adjusted to an OD600 nm of 0.6 in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 150 μM acetosyringone and 10 mM MES, pH 5.6). Equal volumes of Agrobacteria carrying pairs of nLUC and cLUC constructs of interest and controls were co-infiltrated into 4-week-old N. benthamiana leaves. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, 150 μg ml−1 D-luciferin potassium salt (ST196, Beyotime) was sprayed onto the abaxial surface of tobacco leaves, followed by a 3-min dark reaction. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using a PlantView100 multispectral dynamic fluorescence microscope system (BLT Photon Technology).

Industry observers note that for bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays, the full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ lacking the translational stop codon was amplified and cloned into the cYFP vector pSm35s-cYFP (BioRun), whereas the coding sequences lacking the translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 were amplified and cloned into the nYFP vector pSm35s-nYFP (BioRun). The resulting constructs were introduced into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants. The infiltration buffer contained 10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, adjusted to pH 5.6. The bacterial suspension was diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.4 before infiltration. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 514 nm and an emission wavelength range of 525–555 nm.

It has been revealed that the same constructs were transformed into wheat protoplasts, which were incubated for 20 h to allow transient expression. YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus), with nuclei labelled using DAPI. Total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were obtained for SDS–PAGE and western blotting. Western blotting (described below) was performed using the primary antibody anti-GFP tag mouse monoclonal antibody (1:1,000; A02020, Abbkine), followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

It has been revealed that full-length cDNAs of EpTFIIAγ, TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46 were amplified by PCR and cloned into the pMAL-c5X vector (for MBP tagging), pET32a (Novagen; for His or HA tagging) or the pGEX4T-1 vector (Merck; for GST-tagged expression) using the ClonExpress II One-Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme) following the manufacturers’ instructions and lacking the respective translational start or stop codons as required. The resulting recombinant plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli Rosetta and cultured in LB medium supplemented with ampicillin at 37 °C. When the culture reached OD600 nm of 0.4–0.6, protein expression was induced by adding 0.5 mM isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation at 16 °C for 14–16 h. The expressed proteins and corresponding controls were subsequently purified using the GST-tag Protein Purification Kit (P2253, Beyotime), anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) or Dextrin beads 6FF (SA026100, Smart-Lifesciences) according to the respective manufacturer’s protocols. The proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected with anti-HA (AH158-IgG1, Beyotime), anti-GST (AM926, Beyotime) and anti-MBP (66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group) antibodies, respectively.

MBP-tagged EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were individually incubated with GST, GST–TaAKS1, GST–TaWRKY46, GST–TaARF6, HA–TaVOZ1, GST–TaTFIIAαβ or GST–AtTFIIAαβ at 4 °C for 3 h. Protein complexes were immunoprecipitated using BeyoGold GST-tag purification resin (P2253, Beyotime) or anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) at 4 °C for 4 h. After incubation, complexes were collected by centrifugation at 300g for 5 min, followed by five washes with phosphate-buffered saline. Proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected by western blotting (described below) using anti-GST antibody (1:1,000 dilution; AM926, Beyotime), anti-HA antibody (1:1,000 dilution, AF2305, Beyotime) and anti-MBP antibody (1:1,000 dilution; 66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group), and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) or goat anti-rabbit IgG (H + L) secondary antibodies (diluted 1:1,000; A0216 and A0208, respectively, Beyotime).

Sources indicate that for co-immunoprecipitation assays, fusion constructs including EpTFIIAγ–GFP, TaAKS1–GFP, TaARF6–mCherry, TaWRKY46–mCherry, EpTFIIAγ–mCherry and TaVOZ1–GFP were prepared in pCAMBIA1302 and pICH86988 vectors, respectively. Combinations of these constructs were co-transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101, which was subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of N. benthamiana in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, pH of 5.6). After 48 h of transient expression, total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P1015, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were incubated with GFP-Trap beads (GTA-20, ChromoTek) at 4 °C for 3 h with gentle rotation. Corresponding protein complexes were obtained after a series of washing steps and elution steps. Input and eluted proteins were then resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Western blotting was performed using primary antibodies to GFP (1:2,000; AE012, Abclonal) or mCherry (1:1,000; ABM40125, Abbkine), followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

EpTFIIAγ and SEUSS69 were cloned into the pET-15b expression vector (for His tagging) and heterologously expressed in E. coli Rosetta cells. The recombinant proteins were purified using NTA-Ni magnetic agarose beads with the His-Tag Protein Purification Kit (P2247S, Beyotime) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For phase-separation assays, purified proteins were diluted to 10 μM in phase-separation buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM dithiothreitol). 10% PEG8000 was included as a molecular crowding agent to promote condensate formation. Samples were gently mixed and equilibrated at room temperature before imaging. Condensates were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) equipped with a ×60 oil-immersion objective (NA = 1.42) and images were processed using FV31S-SW software.

It has been revealed that protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay kit (PA115-02, Tiangen Biotech). SDS–PAGE was performed with a PAGE Gel Fast Preparation Kit (EpiZyme). Protein samples (obtained from either prokaryotic expression, in vitro and in planta validation) were mixed with 5× SDS loading buffer at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. Ten micrograms of protein sample and 5 μl of 10–180 kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) were loaded onto gels. Electrophoresis was run at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. For wet transfer, the gel, 0.45-μm PVDF membrane and filter papers were soaked in transfer buffer (PS109, EpiZyme) for 15 min to equilibrate. A transfer stack was assembled, and transfer was conducted at a constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C. Post-transfer, the PVDF membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in transfer buffer; PS109, EpiZyme) on a shaker at room temperature for 2 h. The membrane was then incubated with primary antibody (1:1,000 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk, adjusted per antibody instructions) on a shaker at 4 °C overnight. After three washes with TBST (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 0.1% (v/v) Tween-20), the membrane was incubated with 1:1,000 HRP-labelled secondary antibody (diluted in 5% w/v non-fat milk) at room temperature for 1.5 h. The membrane was washed three times with TBST and once with TBS for 5 min. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using ECL substrate (34098CN, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after 2 min of dark incubation, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system.

Transgenic wheat, rice, maize and Arabidopsis plants, along with non-transgenic controls, were used for the assay for EpTFIIAγ abundance. The anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody was generated by Genecreate via rabbit immunization with EpTFIIAγ-specific short polypeptides, and its specificity was verified by western blotting. Seedlings of rice, maize and wheat were grown to the three-leaf stage under the aforementioned culture conditions; Arabidopsis seedlings were grown for 2 weeks. For each plant, 2 g of leaves were weighed, quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into powder in a pre-cooled mortar. The powder was transferred to a pre-cooled 50-ml centrifuge tube, and 5 ml of plant RIPA lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (50×; P1055, Beyotime) was added. After resuspension, the mixture was incubated on ice for 30 min, then centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected for subsequent experiments. Protein concentration was determined by the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) method. A total of 15–20 μg of protein was mixed with 5× SDS–PAGE sample loading buffer (P0015, Beyotime) at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. SDS–PAGE was performed with a 12% separating gel: electrophoresis at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. A 10–180-kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) was used as a reference. Proteins were transferred to a 0.45-μm PVDF membrane by wet transfer (constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C for 90 min). The membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in TBST) at room temperature for 2 h, then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody (1:500 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk). After three washes with TBST, the membrane was incubated with HRP-labelled goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (A0208, Beyotime) at 1:5,000 dilution for 1 h at room temperature. Following three additional TBST washes, the membrane was developed with ECL chemiluminescent substrate, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system. The target protein expression level was analysed based on the presence of the target band. Actin was used as a loading control, detected with an anti-actin antibody (AA128, Beyotime) and HRP-labelled goat anti-mouse secondary antibody (A0216, Beyotime).

According to recent reports, total protein was extracted from seedling leaves using plant protein extraction buffer (AS08300, Agrisera). Equal amounts of protein (10 μg) were resolved by 12.5% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Amersham, GE Healthcare). Membranes were probed with primary antibodies to Cyt b6 (AS184069, Agrisera), PsbA (AS05084, Agrisera), PsbD (AS06146, Agrisera), AtpB (AS05085, Agrisera), RbcL (AS03037, Agrisera), RbcS (AS07259, Agrisera), Lhca2 (AS01006, Agrisera) and Lhcb2 (AS01003, Agrisera) at the recommended dilutions, followed by incubation with a goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:10,000; AS09602, Agrisera). Actin (AA128, Beyotime) served as the loading control, and protein signals were visualized using the standard chemiluminescence detection described above.

Sources indicate that three-leaf-stage seedling leaves of transgenic wheat expressing EpTFIIAγ–HA in the cv. Fielder background were collected and used for ChIP as previously described70. In brief, 2 g of plant tissue was washed twice with cold phosphate-buffered saline buffer and crosslinked with 1% v/v formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature. The crosslinking was quenched by adding glycine to a final concentration of 125 mM. Samples were then lysed in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 10 mM EDTA, 1% w/v SDS and protease inhibitor cocktail. Chromatin was extracted on ice and sonicated to obtain soluble, sheared fragments with an average DNA length of 200–500 bp. A 20-μl aliquot was reserved as the input control and stored at –20 °C, whereas 100 μl of the sheared chromatin was used for immunoprecipitation with 10 μg of anti-HA antibody (ChIP grade, ab9110, Abcam) overnight at 4 °C. Subsequently, 30 μl of protein A/G magnetic beads was added, followed by incubation for 3 h. Beads were sequentially washed with low-salt buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 50 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% v/v Triton X-100 and 0.1% w/v SDS), twice with high-salt buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 250 mM LiCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% v/v NP-40 and 1% w/v deoxycholic acid), and twice with TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 1 mM EDTA). Chromatin was eluted in 300 μl of elution buffer (100 mM NaHCO3 and 1% w/v SDS), treated with RNase A (8 μg ml−1) at 65 °C for 6 h, followed by proteinase K (345 μg ml−1) digestion overnight at 45 °C. Immunoprecipitated DNA was then used to prepare sequencing libraries using the NEXTFLEX ChIP–seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NOVA-5143-02, Bioo Scientific) and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using a paired-end 150-bp strategy.

Low-quality sequencing reads were filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome (IWGSC RefSeq v1.1) using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72. SAMtools (v1.3.1)73 was used to remove PCR duplicates from the aligned data. MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 was used for peak calling using default parameters (bandwidth = 300 bp; model fold = 5, 50; q value = 0.05). Each peak was assigned to the gene for the TSS of which was closest to the peak midpoint. Motif analysis within the peaks was conducted using HOMER (v3)75 with default settings and a maximum motif length of 12 bp. Gene Ontology functional enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler package in R76. Statistical significance was determined using a hypergeometric test with a P value threshold of 0.05.

To validate ChIP–seq results, ChIP–qPCR was performed. One microlitre of purified ChIP DNA was used as template in a 20-μl qPCR containing SYBR Green Master Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme). Amplification was carried out using a Bio-Rad CFX96 real-time PCR system. Primers were designed to amplify genomic regions containing predicted binding sites based on ChIP–seq results. Each qPCR was conducted in four times. Enrichment values were calculated as mean ± s.d. from three biological replicates and are presented. Non-specific IgG and primers targeting intergenic regions were included as negative controls. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

Total RNA was extracted from leaves of wild-type Fielder and two EpTFIIAγ–HA transgenic lines (TL4 and TL7) using TRIzol reagent (15596026, Invitrogen). Genomic DNA was removed by DNase I treatment following extraction. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a Nanodrop OneC Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) by examining the A260:A280 ratio. RNA integrity was confirmed through 1.5% w/v agarose gel electrophoresis and quantified using a Qubit 3.0 fluorometer with the Qubit RNA Broad Range Assay kit (Q10210, Life Technologies). For library construction, 2 μg of total RNA was used to prepare strand-specific RNA-seq libraries with the KC Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (DR08402, Wuhan Seqhealth), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were enriched for fragments ranging from 200 to 500 bp, quantified and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform using paired-end reads.

According to recent reports, raw sequencing reads were quality filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71 to remove adapter sequences and low-quality reads. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome IWGSC RefSeq (v1.1) using GEM (v2.5)77. PCR duplicates were removed, and gene expression levels were quantified using DESeq2 (ref. 78). DEGs were identified using a threshold of |log2 (fold change)| > 1 and P < 0.05. Gene Ontology classification and enrichment analysis of DEGs were conducted using the clusterProfiler package76, identifying statistically significantly enriched terms among upregulated and downregulated genes.

Industry observers note that paired-end CUT&Tag79 reads were quality filtered with fastp80 and aligned to the wheat cv. Fielder reference genome using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72 in end-to-end, very-sensitive mode. Reads with mapping quality < 20 were removed, and duplicate reads were removed after processing with samtools fixmate and samtools markdup73. Genome-wide RPKM-normalized bigWig tracks were generated with deepTools bamCoverage, and signal enrichment around genes and TSSs was visualized using computeMatrix and plotHeatmap81. Peaks were called for each replicate with MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 using matched IgG/input controls. Reproducible peaks between biological replicates were identified using IDR82 and used as consensus peaks. Consensus peaks were annotated against the Fielder genome annotation83. Promoter-associated target genes were defined at the peak–gene pair level: a gene was retained only when its own signed distance from the peak to the TSS satisfied distance to TSS ≤ 3 kb. Motif enrichment was performed on promoter peak regions using HOMER75 with sequence extraction and shuffled genomic background generation performed using BEDTools84.

Recent findings suggest that EMSA was performed using the Chemiluminescent EMSA Kit (GS009, Beyotime Biotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Biotin-labelled DNA probes containing putative binding motifs were synthesized by Sangon Biotech and used at a final concentration of 0.05 μM per reaction. Each 20-μl binding reaction contained 4 μl of 5× EMSA/gel-shift binding buffer, 1 μg of recombinant protein (MBP tagged or GST tagged) and the biotin-labelled probe. Reactions were incubated at 23 °C for 30 min, then separated on a native 8% polyacrylamide gel in 0.5× TBE buffer (R0223, Beyontime) at 100 V for 1 h. DNA–protein complexes were transferred onto a nylon membrane (FFN10, Beyontime) and crosslinked by UV. Detection of biotin-labelled DNA was performed using a streptavidin–HRP conjugate and chemiluminescent substrate according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Negative controls included using MBP or GST. Washing and visualization were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

To assess transcriptional regulation mediated by EpTFIIAγ, 1.5-kb promoter regions of selected target genes were cloned into the pGreenII-0800-LUC vector to produce reporter constructs, whereas the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector to produce an effector construct25. Empty pGreenII-0800-LUC and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. LUC and REN activities were subsequently measured using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit (RG027, Beyotime), and relative luciferase activity was calculated as the ratio of LUC-to-REN activity.

According to recent reports, to investigate the effect of EpTFIIAγ on the transcriptional activity of its assayed interacting proteins (TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46), the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pCAMBIA1302 vector, whereas the coding sequences of the transcription factors were cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector. Promoter regions (1.5 kb) of downstream target genes (TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1) were cloned into pGreenII-0800-LUC to generate reporter constructs. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. Luciferase activities were measured as described above, and relative transcriptional activity was determined by calculating the LUC:REN ratio. Empty pCAMBIA1302 and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. All experiments were conducted with at least three biological replicates.

It has been revealed that fungal and plant TFIIAγ candidates were retrieved from the JGI MycoCosm portal85 and the OneKP project86, respectively. Protein-level similarity searches were conducted using EpTFIIAγ and representative TFIIAγ proteins as queries. Partial fragments and sequences with abnormal lengths (outside 70–150 amino acids) were removed. Redundant identical sequences from the same species were collapsed, but distinct isoforms passing the filtering criteria were retained. Ultimately, 3,183 fungal and 1,245 Viridiplantae sequences were included, resulting in a final dataset of 4,428 TFIIAγ proteins (Supplementary Table 7).

Industry observers note that filtered protein sequences were aligned with MAFFT (v7.525)87 using the automatic strategy selection mode. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic inference was performed with IQ-TREE (v3.0.1)88. The best-fitting amino acid substitution model was selected with ModelFinder, and branch support was estimated using 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates and 1,000 Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like approximate likelihood ratio test replicates. The resulting tree was visualized as a circular phylogeny using custom Python scripts with Biopython (v1.84) and Matplotlib (v3.10.8).

Protein structure prediction for TFIIAγ was conducted using AlphaFold3 (ref. 89) for orthologues from E. pusillum (EPUS02736), wheat (TraesCS1D02G024600), rice (LOC_Os01g73890), maize (Zm00001eb356100) and Arabidopsis (AT4G24440) with default parameters, and the resulting models were visualized using PyMOL (v3.1.0).

Recent findings suggest that statistical tests were conducted using two-tailed Student’s t-tests, Kruskal–Wallis tests, one-way ANOVA, and Brown-Forsythe and Welch ANOVA in GraphPad Prism (v9.5.0). Differences were considered statistically significant at *P < 0.05 or **P < 0.01. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. from at least three independent biological replicates or independent experiments unless otherwise specified in legends.

According to recent reports, J.W., Z.K. and H.M. conceived the original idea and designed the early experiments. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the major experimental work. Specifically, L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.W., P.J., Y.H., D.T., S.Y., Q.W., S.T., Z.S., L.S., M.Y., T.X., Y.L., S.Z., P.Z., W.F., J.H., J.Z. and G.Z. contributed to plant cultivation and phenotypic characterization under controlled and field conditions, including stress-resistance phenotyping, agronomic trait assessment, grain-filling analysis and physiological measurements. X.H. generated the transgenic plants. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.T., Z.S., L.S. and J.H. conducted the microscopy and imaging analyses. F.L., H.Z., B.L., C.W., D.T. and Q.W. performed the biochemical and protein-related experiments. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.W., S.W., S.L. and D.T. conducted the molecular and transcriptional regulation assays. B.C., Z.Q. and Y.W. performed the genomic, transcriptomic and computational analyses. L.D. and Z.Q. conducted the phylogenetic analysis and protein structure prediction. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the statistical analyses and data quantification. H.M. and L.D. wrote the manuscript with input from X.Q., J.W. and Z.K. All authors reviewed and approved the final manuscript.

A patent application related to the work described in this article has been filed in China. The patent applicants are the Institute of Microbiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences and Northwest A&F University. The inventors are J.W., Z.K., X.Q., H.M., Xinli Wei, Y.W. and F.L. The application number is 202111602359.2, and the patent application is currently under substantive examination. The patent application covers the use of the extremophile gene EpTFIIAγ for improving abiotic stress resistance in wheat, rice and maize. The other authors declare no other competing interests.

Kean’s newly introduced tibia injury rules former Juventus striker out of Como v Juventus

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Moise Kean has broken down again in Como training, three weeks after treatment that was meant to fix his shin.
  • According to recent reports, moise Kean has suffered a fresh tibia injury in training with Como.
  • Sources indicate that como’s statement of 17 November gave no recovery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moise Kean has broken down again in Como training, three weeks after treatment that was meant to fix his shin. The former Juventus striker is set to miss about two more months, so he will not face his old club on 29 November.

According to recent reports, moise Kean has suffered a fresh tibia injury in training with Como. The former Juventus striker is now undergoing further medical tests. Sky Sport Italia reported that he will be out for about two more months. That timeline rules him out of Como’s home game against Juventus.

Sources indicate that como’s statement of 17 November gave no recovery date. The club promised an patch once more information was available.

In a recent development, the upcoming problem follows a treatment that was meant to end his shin trouble. On 30 October, Como’s update described his treatment at the Cugat Institute in Barcelona as successful. The club put his recovery at about five weeks. His progress was to be reviewed every day.

That initiative has now collapsed. Kean had been out since early October. The original injury came while he was playing for Italy against France on 2 October. That match was the first leg of a Nations League tie.

The setback is a heavy blow for Como. In Serie A, his outings for the club added up to 160 minutes. He has yet to score, including in his single Champions League game. He joined from Fiorentina on an initial loan, with an obligation to make the move permanent. At Fiorentina he scored 27 league goals in two seasons, 19 of them in 2024/25. Before that, he came through the Juventus academy.

It has been revealed that without him, Como will have to rely on Douvikas up front. The club may also look for a striker in January.

For Juventus, the news removes one threat from a crucial stretch. Como are their next opponents after Venezia. The game is the Sunday evening fixture a week later, in round 13 of Serie A. Kick-off is at 20:45.

Como 1907 is pleased to announce the signing of Italian international forward Moise Kean from @acffiorentina on an initial loan, with an obligation to make the move permanent.

Official statement ➡️ https://t.co/PJKnFXS9Xp pic.twitter.com/4F30ROYFUT.

— Como1907 (@Como_1907) September 1, 2026.

Industry observers note that luciano Spalletti’s side need results. Juventus sit six points behind fourth place and have averaged just over 1.6 points per game, according to Corriere dello Sport. The paper sees the run of fixtures as decisive for the push for a Champions League place. It warns that dropping points against Venezia would force Juventus to win every remaining game of 2026 to stay in touch with the top four.

The schedule offers little respite after the trip to Como. Juventus host Udinese on 6 December and Monza on 14 December. They then travel to Roma on 19 December.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The relationship between Frenkie de Jong and Hansi Flick has taken a serious hit in recent months, after the Dutchman lost the captain’s armband.
  • Sources indicate that since then, the situation has improved significantly, as reported Sport.
  • In a recent development, manu Tournoux is a passionate and knowledgeable football enthusiast with a special focus on French football.

The relationship between Frenkie de Jong and Hansi Flick has taken a serious hit in recent months, after the Dutchman lost the captain’s armband. The main point of friction concerned the management of his ankle injury: after having forced himself to play the World Cup with his selection, the midfielder went on vacation without going to the Barça medical center. An attitude which greatly displeased the German coach, especially since the doctors recommended an operation, while the player favored conservative treatment. During the summer preparation, Flick even asked him to follow the group’s movements despite his unavailability.

Sources indicate that since then, the situation has improved significantly, as reported Sport. De Jong reportedly made a commitment to his coach to return to his best level and stepped up his efforts: additional sessions, regular medical check-ups and presence at Ciudad Deportiva even on his days off. An involvement which convinced Flick, who once again considers him an essential element of his team. The Dutchman also indicated his versatility by agreeing to play different positions according to the needs of the team. After being used in central defense against Alavés, he helped out at full-back against Atlético de Madrid.
